subject: Contradictory recommendations on separate GPAs for modularity test?

messages.author: c502f192564aca42
messages.subject: Contradictory recommendations on separate GPAs for modularity test?
parts:
Dear All,


With some colleagues we are currently discussing a challenge similar to the one described by Bob in “modularity with different alignments” (https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/6qEiVNQPdaM/m/6yknAfQvAQAJ; i.e. GPA for landmark sets on structures that move relative to each other in preparation for a modularity test). In this context, I also found the discussion in “modularity.test - one landmarks important for multiple modules” (https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/21ODVPFWUmM) very interesting. To me, the recommendations in the two discussions seem to contradict somehow:

- “modularity with different alignments” recommends to use the combine.subsets function (including performing separate GPAs for the different landmark sets?) to deal with landmarks on movable parts to prepare a modularity test.

- “modularity.test - one landmarks important for multiple modules” recommends to not perform separate GPAs.

 

I hope I got the main messages of the two discussions correctly? If so, I am probably missing something important, e.g. that the combine.subsets-function is doing something special or that the cases in the two discussion differ in important prerequisite? I would be very grateful for any explanation on how the recommendations in the two mentioned discussions fit together (e.g., are there any special cases in which GPAs can be performed separately for assumed modules? Can combine.subsets help under certain circumstances? ...).

 

Thank you very much in advance and kind regards!

Karo

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Contradictory recommendations on separate GPAs for modularity test?
parts:
Dear Karo,

The discussions are not contradictory os long as modularity is a test of a single “structure” broken into parts and the combining of subsets means the combining of separate structures.  A modularity test examines whether a single structure behaves as separate structures.  For example, a mammalian skull is a single structure but comprises separate, fused skull bones.  One could test how seemingly independent the separate bones are but if one were to digitize the entire skull (not including the jaw bones), the locations of landmarks are rather fixed; rotating the skull rotates the the landmarks within separate skull bones exactly the same way.  Performing separate GPAs on each of the skull bones allows them to rotate freely, as if they are not fused.  This is a problem.

Alternatively, the morphology of a fish might be defined both by its head shapes (skull and jaw) and tail shape.  One might expect the three separate shapes to be integrated.  Fish with tail shapes that work for active swimming might have skull and jaw bones that facilitate ram feeding.  But the landmarks used to characterize tail shape, skull shape, and jaw shape are not fixed with respect to each other.  One might perform separate GPAs on tails, skulls, and jaws and then combine these subsets of landmarks for a single morphological characterization of separate parts.  A modularity test does not mean much here because the three parts are completely modular, without a test needed to confirm it.  (They could still be integrated modules, but that is a different consideration.)

I ranted in one of those discussions that the recommendation of separate GPAs for modularity tests treats the mammalian skull bones as if they were like jaws, skulls, and tails of fish. Ignoring that they are fused obliterates the spatial covariances among landmarks between hypothesized modules.  However, not treating the fish jaws, skulls, and tails as separate, and attempting to digitize them all as one unit, say in a photograph, means that the arbitrary position of the tail or opening of the jaw become fixed in the same GPA, creating spatial covariances that are not constant in life, unlike the bones of the mammalian skull.

I hope this clears up the confusion.  The separate discussions differed with respect to the number of structures used to characterize an organism’s morphology.   Therefore, whether to use or combine subsets of landmarks was not ambiguous.

Best,
mike

messages.author: c502f192564aca42
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Contradictory recommendations on separate GPAs for modularity test?
parts:
Dear Mike,
 
Thank you very much for the fast and thorough answer!
 
I totally understand that it is not meaningful (wrong) to perform separate GPAs if the landmarks are located on the same “rigid” structure. And I guess I need some more time to digest the case with landmarks on parts that move relative to each other and to get to understand the core principles of modularity testing... ! (e.g. performing separate GPA, to me, seems to virtually disarticulate the respective movable elements and I am not yet sure if I understand how this may affect the covariance within and between the expected modules during the calculation of the covariance ratio or what effects this has on the covariance ration if the “new modules” are randomly assigned during significance testing.) Will work on that, your explanations already help me a lot! Anyway, I think it means for our particular case that it is not meaningful to test for modularity and we will consider testing for integration instead.
 
Just because of pure curiosity and with regard to the example of fish jaws and skulls you mentioned: Would it be possible (meaningful) to standardize the angle between jaws and skulls (e.g. with geomorph::fixed.angle), perform one GPA for all landmarks, and then test for modularity?
 
Again, thank you very much and kind regards,
Karo

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Contradictory recommendations on separate GPAs for modularity test?
parts:
Dear Karo,

Just for clarity, I am not sure (or would have to be convinced otherwise) that a test of modularity for separate structures should be performed.  They are modular, by definition.  The only way one might hope to do this is make sure that the orientation and spatial locations of centroids of different structures are fixed in some way.  Then, perhaps, one could test for modularity with caveats (could be just a result of the pre-defined orientation and fixing of centroids) but even if that were possible, one could not ascertain how modular their modularity is.  I would recommend against trying to do this.

As for a test of integration, it does not matter that structures are independent and in a strange way, it is almost comforting.  Unlike a single structure broken into hypothesized modules, one does not have to contend with the strong covariances between proximate landmarks that just happened to be assigned to different modules, masquerading as strong integration when they could contribute to strong modularity by simply altering the composition of modules, even slightly.  For example, in the pupfish example used for modularity.test, the operculum and pectoral fin might be either highly integrated or compose a module, and this is difficult to tell because they are located right next to each other.  Something like a mammal skull and long bone might be integrated, but one does not have to worry that their proximity can complicate this interpretation.

Just because of pure curiosity and with regard to the example of fish jaws and skulls you mentioned: Would it be possible (meaningful) to standardize the angle between jaws and skulls (e.g. with geomorph::fixed.angle), perform one GPA for all landmarks, and then test for modularity?

Sure, it is possible, but if you fix the angle say three different ways and get three different measures of modularity, what confidence do you have that you have detected and appropriately measured it?  What if you get significant results with one angle but not another? 

The problem is this arbitrary step creates a covariance matrix that is fixed and the only alteration in random permutations of a modularity test is the locations of the covariances in the matrix.  You could create or ablate modularity by an arbitrary decision on how to fix the angle.

Maybe if you performed an analysis wehere you changed the angle, say one degree at a time, over a realistic range of angles, and keep getting consistent modularity results, then you might have some confidence that you did not just manufacture it, arbitrarily.

Again, thank you very much and kind regards,
Karo
